SUBPATH ROBOTS CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your sitemap ever actually read?

A crawler fetches robots.txt from exactly one place: the origin root. If your site lives under a path prefix — user.github.io/repo/, group.gitlab.io/project/, a CDN subdirectory — then the robots.txt you publish is at an address nothing ever requests, and the Sitemap: line inside it is never seen. Your pages are never enumerated. Nothing errors when this happens, which is why it usually goes unnoticed for years.

Nothing is uploaded. What you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this page makes no network calls — not even to fetch the robots.txt it tells you about.

1. Where is your site published?

Paste the address of your site's home page. A trailing index.html is fine — it is read as the directory it sits in.

Enter a URL above and click Check.

2. Optional: paste the robots.txt files

The check above works from the URL alone. These two make the report more specific, and the second one is the only way to find out whether a file you do not control is blocking you outright.

Add robots.txt contents

Reports which of its directives are inert.

Open the origin-root URL the report names, copy what is there, and paste it here. A 404 means no file exists, which crawlers read as no restrictions — leave this blank in that case.

Result

Run it in CI instead

Zero dependencies, Node 18+. It opens no sockets at all unless you pass --fetch.

node cli.mjs check https://your-name.github.io/your-repo/
node cli.mjs check https://your-name.github.io/your-repo/ --fetch --fail-on-critical
node cli.mjs explain

--fail-on-critical exits 1 when the governing file is not yours, so a deploy pipeline can refuse to ship a site whose pages will never be enumerated.

Questions people actually ask

Why is my GitHub Pages sitemap never read?

Crawlers fetch robots.txt from one fixed place: the origin root. A project site at user.github.io/repo/ publishes its robots.txt at user.github.io/repo/robots.txt, which nothing ever requests, so the Sitemap: line inside it is never seen and the sitemap is never fetched.

Does this mean my pages are not indexed at all?

No. Crawling by following links is unaffected — any page linked from a page a crawler already knows can still be found and indexed. What breaks is enumeration: pages that only appear in the sitemap and are not linked from a crawled page are never discovered. That is why the failure is silent, since some pages do get indexed.

Whose robots.txt actually governs a GitHub Pages project site?

The one served by the repository named <user>.github.io — the account's user or organization site. If that repository does not exist, GitHub returns 404 for the file, which crawlers treat as no restrictions. Either way, a project site cannot put a Sitemap: line anywhere a crawler will read it.

Can I at least block a crawler from my subpath site?

Not with robots.txt. A Disallow: you write in a subpath robots.txt is as inert as the Sitemap: line. Use a per-page <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> tag or an X-Robots-Tag header instead — those need no origin-root file.

Does a clean result mean my site's SEO is fine?

No. This checks one specific, mechanical thing: whether the robots.txt a crawler reads is the one your site publishes, and what follows for sitemap discovery. It is not an SEO audit and says nothing about your content, your links, or whether any search engine has chosen to index you.

More on the mechanism, and the full list of what this cannot tell you: why a subpath site cannot govern its robots.txt, or how this compares to just opening robots.txt and reading it.

vs-checking-robots-txt-by-eye.html.text:
← back to the checker

This checker vs. opening robots.txt and looking

The obvious way to check your robots.txt is to open it in a browser tab and read it. That works for what it checks: is the file syntactically sane, does it say what you meant. It does not answer the question that actually determines whether your sitemap gets read, because the file most people open by habit — the one at their own site's address — is usually not the file a crawler fetches at all.

What each one is for

Opening robots.txt and reading it is free and needs no tool: paste the URL, look at the text. It correctly answers "is this file well-formed" and "does this rule say what I think it says", for whichever file you happened to open.

This checker starts from your site's URL rather than a robots.txt URL, works out which file actually governs it under RFC 9309 (always the origin root, never a path prefix), and reports the gap when the two differ. Paste the origin-root file too, and it applies the longest-match-wins rule for you rather than leaving it to be eyeballed.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is the robots.txt I publish syntactically correct?Either one. Opening it and reading it answers this directly, and so does this checker's inert-directive report.
Is the file I just read the one a crawler actually fetches?This checker. The file at your own site's address is the governing file only when your site is at an origin root — otherwise it is a different URL you have to know to check.
Does a rule in the origin-root file block my path outright?This checker, applying RFC 9309's longest-match rule to whatever you paste, rather than reading it by eye.
Will my Sitemap: line ever be auto-discovered?This checker's core question. A file that looks correct when opened can still be a file nothing requests.
Is anything I paste uploaded anywhere?Neither. Opening a URL involves no third party beyond the site itself, and this checker makes no network calls of its own.

Common questions

I opened my robots.txt in a browser and it looks fine — isn't that enough?

It confirms the file you publish is syntactically correct, which is a real thing to check. It does not confirm that file is the one a crawler reads. The URL you probably opened is your site's own robots.txt under its path prefix — exactly the file this tool exists to point out gets fetched by nothing.

What would I have to do by hand to actually answer the governance question?

Work out your site's origin root from the URL, open robots.txt there instead of at your own path, and read it for a Disallow rule that matches your path prefix — applying RFC 9309's longest-match-wins rule, where Allow only wins a tie. That is a different file, a different question, and a rule most people have not memorized, which is exactly why a step of it gets skipped.

Can eyeballing the origin-root file catch a rule that blocks my path?

It can, if you know to check that specific file and apply the longest-match rule correctly. It is easy to get backwards: a shorter Disallow and a longer, more specific Allow both matching your path resolve to Allow, not to whichever rule is read first or looks more prominent.

Does checking by eye ever catch something this tool does not?

Yes — whether the file reads naturally, whether a comment explains an unusual rule, anything about tone or intent. This tool checks one mechanical question: which file governs, and what follows for sitemap discovery. It is not a substitute for reading the file that does apply.

Is anything pasted into either process uploaded?

Opening a URL in a browser tab involves no third party beyond the site itself. This checker runs entirely in your browser too and makes no network calls of its own — not even to fetch the robots.txt files it reports on.

They are not a security audit, a compliance attestation, or a guarantee about your site's search visibility. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

This page names no specific product. "Opening robots.txt and reading it" describes a manual habit every developer already has access to, not any company's product or service.

why-a-subpath-site-cannot-govern-its-rob.text:
← Subpath Robots Check

Why a subpath site cannot govern its robots.txt

Everything below follows from one sentence in the standard, and the consequence is worth more attention than the rule, because it is invisible from inside the site it affects.

Where exactly does a crawler look for robots.txt?

At the origin root, and nowhere else. RFC 9309 §2.3 fixes the location as scheme://host:port/robots.txt. The file is scoped to the origin, so one file governs every path on that host, and no per-directory file is ever consulted.

That is a deliberate design choice, not an oversight. A crawler would otherwise have to fetch and merge a file for every directory it descends into, and the rules could contradict each other at different depths.

The practical result is that a site published under a path prefix inherits a policy file it did not write and cannot edit:

https://acme.github.io/widget/       <- your site
https://acme.github.io/robots.txt    <- the file that governs it
https://acme.github.io/widget/robots.txt  <- fetched by nothing

What does this actually cost?

Sitemap auto-discovery, which is the mechanism that enumerates pages. A crawler finds a sitemap by reading the Sitemap: line out of the governing robots.txt. A sitemap advertised only from a subpath is therefore never fetched, and the URLs listed in it are never discovered that way.

There is a second cost that runs the other direction, and people notice it even less: a Disallow: written in a subpath robots.txt is equally inert. A draft section you thought you had excluded from search is not excluded from anything.

What does it not cost?

Crawling by following links, which is entirely unaffected. Any page linked from a page the crawler already knows is still reached and can still be indexed.

That is precisely why this failure is hard to spot. Some pages do get indexed. Nothing returns an error. Every tool that checks the origin root finds a perfectly healthy robots.txt — it just belongs to someone else. The gap only shows up as a slow, unexplained shortfall between how many pages you published and how many were ever found.

A measured instance

The portfolio that publishes this tool has the same defect, on the same day this page was written, and says so in its own repository rather than quietly. Its catalogue of several hundred free tools is served from a GitHub Pages project subpath; the Sitemap: line it publishes is at an address no crawler requests; and its own deployment check reports the condition as subpath-robots every time it runs.

That is the honest version of a case study: not a claim that the tool found a customer's problem, but a statement that the problem is real, current, and cost the people writing this the same thing it may be costing you.

Is a custom domain really the only complete fix?

It is the only one that restores auto-discovery itself, because it moves the site to an origin root where its own robots.txt governs. The alternatives are real and worth doing, but they are per-search-engine pushes rather than a repair to the discovery mechanism:

OptionWhat it fixesWhat it does not
Custom domainEverything here. Your robots.txt governs, auto-discovery works, your Disallow: rules apply.Costs a domain registration and a DNS record.
Direct sitemap submissionEnumeration, for the search engines you submit to.Needs a verified account per engine; covers only those engines.
IndexNowFast notification of new and changed URLs, no account needed.Google does not consume it. Bing, Yandex and Seznam do.
A complete internal link graphDiscovery, via the route that still works.Slower than a sitemap, and needs at least one inbound link from an already-crawled page.
meta name="robots"Exclusion, reliably and per page.Nothing about discovery. It is the answer to the other half of the problem.

What this tool cannot tell you

Stated plainly, because a checker that implies more than it measures is worse than none:

  • Whether any search engine has actually indexed your pages. It reasons about mechanism, never about a search engine's decisions.
  • How a specific crawler behaves in practice. Compliance with RFC 9309 is voluntary, and implementations differ in the details.
  • Whether your content ranks. Discovery is a precondition for ranking, not a cause of it.
  • What a robots.txt you have not pasted contains. The browser page makes no network calls at all; the CLI fetches only with --fetch, and only the origin-root file.
  • Whether a non-compliant crawler honours anything at all. Some ignore robots.txt entirely, which is outside what any checker can observe.
  • Anything about hosts it has no specific knowledge of. GitHub Pages and GitLab Pages are named because their ownership model is documented; every other host is reported as a generic subpath without inventing an owner for it.
